# The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
## 1 Introduction
Our paper provides the first economy-wide and cross-model evidence of the effects of agentic AI on the labor market, and specifically on job postings. We combine and match two datasets. The first is the proprietary data from OpenRouter that contains granular information on about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (1.1 quadrillion tokens of agentic realized AI consumption) across more than 400 models and covers millions of users---about two percent of global realized token consumption, the largest dataset of cross-model AI token consumption.

The resulting agentic betas capture public firms’ market-implied sensitivity to growth in realized aggregate agentic AI token consumption.

ceramic.title: State of AI 2025: 100T Token LLM Usage Study | OpenRouter
ceramic.snippet:
The past year has marked a turning point in the evolution and real-world use of large language models (LLMs). With the release of the first widely adopted reasoning model,  o1 , on December 5th, 2024, the field shifted from single-pass pattern generation to multi-step deliberation inference, accelerating deployment, experimentation, and new classes of applications. As this shift unfolded at a rapid pace, our empirical understanding of how these models have actually been used in practice has lagged behind. In this work, we leverage the OpenRouter platform, which is an AI inference provider across a wide variety of LLMs, to analyze over 100 trillion tokens of real-world LLM interactions across tasks, geographies, and time. In our empirical study, we observe substantial adoption of open-weight models, the outsized popularity of creative roleplay (beyond just the productivity tasks many assume dominate) and coding assistance categories, plus the rise of agentic inference. Furthermore, our retention analysis identifies  foundational cohorts : early users whose engagement persists far longer than later cohorts. We term this phenomenon the Cinderella  \"Glass Slipper\" effect. These findings underscore that the way developers and end-users engage with LLMs \"in the wild\" is complex and multifaceted. We discuss implications for model builders, AI developers, and infrastructure providers, and outline how a data-driven understanding of usage can inform better design and deployment of LLM systems.

   3. Agents vs Humans: The Rise of Agentic Inference. LLM usage is shifting from single-turn interactions to  agentic inference , where models plan, reason, and execute across multiple steps. Rather than producing one-off responses, they now coordinate tool calls, access external data, and iteratively refine outputs to achieve a goal. Early evidence shows rising multi-step queries and chained tool use that we proxy to agentic use.

### OpenRouter Platform and Dataset

Our analysis is based on metadata collected from the OpenRouter platform, a unified AI inference layer that connects users and developers to hundreds of large language models. Each user request on OpenRouter is executed against a user-selected model, and structured metadata describing the resulting "generation" event is logged. The dataset used in this study consists of anonymized request-level metadata for billions of prompt–completion pairs from a global user base, spanning approximately two years up to the time of writing. We do zoom in on the last year.

Crucially, we did not have access to the underlying text of prompts or completions. Our analysis relies entirely on metadata that capture the structure, timing, and context of each generation, without exposing user content. This privacy-preserving design enables large-scale behavioral analysis.

Each generation record includes information on timing, model and provider identifiers, token usage, and system performance metrics. Token counts encompass both prompt (input) and completion (output) tokens, allowing us to measure overall model workload and cost. Metadata also include fields related to geographic routing, latency, and usage context (for example, whether the request was streamed or cancelled, or whether tool-calling features were invoked). Together, these attributes provide a detailed but non-textual view of how models are used in practice.

If you want a clean read on where AI is heading, look at the inference. Chris Clark, COO and co-founder of OpenRouter, runs the largest AI gateway in the world: around 70 model providers, hundreds of models, one integration that keeps working no matter which lab, cloud, or modality wins next. That vantage point comes with a number that lands hard. OpenRouter expects to process about 28 trillion tokens in a single week. That is roughly 1 percent of all global inference, and more than Salesforce has processed in the entire lifetime of the company.

Half that volume is US and half is the rest of the world, which makes their data a fair proxy for real global trends. And the trend that matters for every B2B founder is the one Clark put front and center.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oxWLDDi_oNU)

## Agentic usage overtook human usage

For two years the message was go make AI work for your company, and it was hard. People chatted with models, dropped some custom data into a project, and got modest results. In OpenRouter’s data, agentic token usage is now overtaking human usage, and you do not need the chart to feel it. Everyone building right now feels it.

## Abstract

The past year has marked a turning point in the evolution and real-world use of large language models (LLMs). With the release of the first widely adopted reasoning model,_o1_, on December 5th, 2024, the field shifted from single-pass pattern generation to multi-step deliberation inference, accelerating deployment, experimentation, and new classes of applications. As this shift unfolded at a rapid pace, our empirical understanding of how these models have actually been used in practice has lagged behind. In this work, we leverage the OpenRouter platform, which is an AI inference provider across a wide variety of LLMs, to analyze over 100 trillion tokens of real-world LLM interactions across tasks, geographies, and time. In our empirical study, we observe substantial adoption of open-weight models, the outsized popularity of creative roleplay (beyond just the productivity tasks many assume dominate) and coding assistance categories, plus the rise of agentic inference. Furthermore, our retention analysis identifies _foundational cohorts_: early users whose engagement persists far longer than later cohorts. We term this phenomenon the Cinderella _"Glass Slipper"_ effect. These findings underscore that the way developers and end-users engage with LLMs "in the wild" is complex and multifaceted. We discuss implications for model builders, AI developers, and infrastructure providers, and outline how a data-driven understanding of usage can inform better design and deployment of LLM systems.

OpenRouter data reveals a major shift in how AI is actually being used.

By August 10, 2026, agentic AI workloads were consuming approximately 7.3 trillion tokens on a 7-day average — compared with roughly 1.4 trillion tokens from human-driven usage.

That means AI agents were using more than 5× as many tokens as humans across OpenRouter’s observed traffic.

The turning point came around February 6, 2026, when agentic token consumption first moved ahead of human usage. Since then, agentic usage has exploded by roughly 14×, rising from around 0.5 trillion to 7.3 trillion tokens.

Why is this happening?

Unlike a traditional chatbot interaction where a human asks a question and receives an answer, an AI agent can work through a task autonomously — reasoning through multiple steps, calling tools, interacting with software, writing and debugging code, searching for information, evaluating results, and repeatedly calling models until the task is complete.

Every additional loop can generate more inference.

So this isn't simply a story about people using AI more.

It signals a deeper transition from AI as a conversational tool → AI as an autonomous worker running continuous workflows.

And because agentic systems can make repeated model and tool calls without a human prompting every step, automated workflows are increasingly becoming a major source of AI inference demand.

One important caveat: these numbers represent OpenRouter's observed traffic, not the entire global AI industry. But the direction is hard to ignore: machines are increasingly generating AI demand for other machines.

keenable.snippet:
We measure agentic AI consumption as the tokens associated with responses that end by calling such tools. Our constructed agentic factor is the aggregate weekly log growth of this token consumption.

We define the agentic factor as the weekly log growth of aggregate agentic tokens.33 3 We define a week to be from Monday to Sunday. For each model response, OpenRouter records whether the model ends its turn by calling an external software tool. Tool calls allow models to request actions such as querying a database, running code, or reading or writing a file. We define *agentic tokens* as the tokens associated with responses that end in a tool call. The agentic factor has a weekly standard deviation of about 36 percent. Additionally, in order to measure broad AI token consumption as opposed to agentic AI-specific token consumption, we consider the AI factor of Borri et al. (2026), defined as the first principal component of standardized weekly log growth in total tokens, dollar expenditure, and the weekly average number of daily active users.

keenable.title: The Cross-Section of Stock Returns and AI Exposure
keenable.snippet:
The paper has four main parts. First, we build a high-frequency, time-varying AI factor from the full universe of OpenRouter AI token consumption data and decompose it into its important components: frontier closed-source versus open-weight models, core versus new users, seasoned versus casual users, long versus short prompts, prompt-content categories (e.g., programming, science, roleplay), and agentic versus ordinary requests. The AI factor and its different components show that the diffusion is uneven, token consumption is concentrated in programming, technology, and sciences, and the share of agentic tokens increased dramatically from negligible to more than half of total AI consumption.

Finally, we provide early evidence on the rise and market-implied effect of agentic AI consumption, defined as models executing multi-step workflows that plan, call external tools, take actions, and coordinate with other agents (see, e.g., Hassabis and Kavukcuoglu, 2024; Ng, 2024a; Ng, 2024b; Yang, Yonack, Zyskowski, Yarats, Ho and Ma, 2025). We measure this component in the OpenRouter data as requests in which the model invokes an external tool. We document the rise in the agentic token share from near zero in 2024 to roughly half of all tokens by the end of the sample, and the agentic dollar share rises more slowly as the realized price per agentic token falls. The granularity of the OpenRouter data allows us to track three salient token-level components of this activity: tool calls, the model’s internal reasoning tokens, and cache reads of recurring prompt prefixes. We show that tool-call and cache-read shares rise to roughly two-fifths to one-half of total token consumption, while reasoning tokens rise more slowly.

We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI
on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion
tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more
than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million
U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level expo-

a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm’s exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower
growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months.

OpenRouter, the unified API gateway that lets developers tap into more than 400 large language models through a single interface, has seen its weekly token usage grow by roughly 9,000x since January 2024. Agentic Inference: We investigate the emergence of multi-step, tool-assisted inference patterns, capturing how users increasingly employ models as components in larger automated systems rather than for single-turn interactions.
A foundational shift is underway in how language models are used in production: from single-turn text completion toward multi-step, tool-integrated, and reasoning-intensive workflows. We refer to this shift as the rise of agentic inference, where models are deployed not just to generate text, but to act through planning, calling tools, or interacting across extended contexts.
On the supply side, the release of higher-capability systems like GPT-5, Claude 4.5, and Gemini 3 expanded what users could expect from stepwise reasoning. On the demand side, users increasingly prefer models that can manage task state, follow multi-step logic, and support agent-style workflows rather than simply generate text.
Together, these trends (rising reasoning share, expanded tool use, longer sequences, and programming's outsize complexity) suggest that the center of gravity in LLM usage has shifted. The median LLM request is no longer a simple question or isolated instruction. Instead, it is part of a structured, agent-like loop, invoking external tools, reasoning over state, and persisting across longer contexts.

[2026-08-24 · by TechDogs · image]

AI agents are consuming nearly 5X as many tokens as humans on OpenRouter, signaling a major shift in where AI compute demand is coming from. 

On February 6, 2026, agent-generated tokens overtook human-generated tokens on the platform for the first time. 

Six months later, agents were generating around 7.3 trillion tokens per week, versus roughly 1.5 trillion for humans. 

Agent usage has grown about 14X since February, while human token consumption has increased much more gradually. 

The difference comes down to how each uses AI. 

A person might send one prompt and read one answer, while an agent can perform hundreds of intermediate actions, including reading files, calling tools, retrying steps, and checking its own work. 

More than 85% of agentic token burn comes from cached prompts, while cached tokens account for nearly all of the relative growth in agent token usage. 

That matters because cached tokens are cheaper than repeatedly processing the original pre-fill, making agent economics increasingly viable, but they remain highly memory-intensive. 

As agents proliferate, demand could therefore shift beyond raw AI adoption toward compute infrastructure, high-bandwidth memory, and eventually even electricity. 

Their rise could also have another consequence: reducing demand for some legacy automation and workflow tools as more tasks are handed directly to autonomous AI systems.

AI is becoming AI's biggest customer as agentic token usage jumps 14x on OpenRouter
  


AI is using more and more AI. According to OpenRouter analyst Peter Walker, February 6, 2026, may have been the last day humans consumed more tokens than AI agents. Agentic token usage has grown 14x since then, while human usage is up just 2.8x. Agents increasingly work on their own over longer stretches, spinning up additional AI processes along the way. But nearly 70 percent of agent token usage comes from cached prompts, which are billed at much lower rates, so actual costs aren't rising as fast as the raw numbers suggest.
 
OpenRouter skews toward open-weight models, which tend to be less token-efficient than models from OpenAI or Anthropic. But the trend likely looks similar at the major labs. Token inflation already started with reasoning models, which think longer before they respond even if they shouldn't.

parallel-fast.snippet:
What the "roughly 5x" figure on OpenRouter actually means

The chart published by a16z classifies token usage on OpenRouter as "agentic," "human," or "mixed," and shows it as a seven-day moving average.
As of August, agentic usage stood at 7.3 trillion tokens and human usage at about 1.4 trillion, a gap of roughly five times.
The key point is that this number is not a comparison of one AI agent and one person doing the same job .
It compares the tokens processed across all of OpenRouter by API usage classified as agentic with the tokens from usage classified as human. It does not directly show the number of users or agents, or how efficiently a single task gets finished.
Also, the 7.3 trillion figure is not a total for the past seven days; it is a usage level expressed as a seven-day moving average.
According to Peter Walker of OpenRouter, who explained the data, agentic token volume overtook human volume on February 6, 2026. Over the following six months or so, agentic usage grew 14-fold. Human usage also grew 2.8-fold over the same period.
In other words, human use of AI did not decline. What grew even faster was a pattern in which a person sets a goal and software keeps working by calling models over and over.
The classification method also deserves attention.
According to Walker's explanation and OpenRouter's official write-up , seven indicators, including tool-call frequency, number of conversation turns, and response intervals, are combined to classify each API key as agentic, mixed, or human.
Individual requests are not labeled one by one as "human" or "agent." If one API key is used for multiple purposes, the whole key is classified by its dominant behavior pattern.
So the "5x" figure does not mean five agents are running per user, nor that a single task needs five times the compute. What it shows is that the makeup of tokens flowing through OpenRouter is tilting rapidly toward agentic use.

seltz.title: OpenRouter October 2026 Data: 790T Tokens, 76% Agents
seltz.snippet:
OpenRouter processed 790T tokens in October 2026, the largest month in its history. Volume rose 37% from September and almost 25x from January, the company said in its October data recap, published on November 6. AI agents used 76% of those tokens.

The recap comes from requests sent through the OpenRouter API, a router that gives developers one key for hundreds of models. It shows where agent traffic goes, what tokens cost and which labs are winning users. Agents are the place to start, since they now drive most of the volume.

## How agents took over OpenRouter traffic

A year ago, agentic API keys took 8% of tokens on OpenRouter. In October they took 76%, or about 600T tokens. OpenRouter credits much of the October jump to the refresh of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The launch of Haiku 5.5 and the rest of the Claude 5.5 family added more.

The label "agentic" is OpenRouter's own. It scores every API key on seven signals, including tool-call rate, turns per request, cache hit rate and time between requests. A key that scores 0.50 or higher counts as an agent.

Agents resend the same long context on every turn, so prompt caching matters more for them. The median cache hit rate on agentic traffic rose from 76.1% in June to over 90% in October. Most providers served cached prefixes for 85 to 97% of agentic prompt tokens.

That cheap, repeated traffic favors cheap models, which is where open weights come in.

## Open-weight models hold the token lead

Open-weight models briefly lost ground in late September. Their share of paid tokens fell to 52% in the week of September 28, when Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol all launched. Two weeks later it was back above 70%, primarily due to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. We ran that model in our DeepSeek V4.1 Flash test, where four Three.js scenes cost $0.15.

Spend tells a different story. Open weights take about a quarter of paid spend on OpenRouter, up from 11% in January.

ultimate.title: The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
ultimate.snippet:
We measure agentic AI consumption as the tokens associated with responses that end by calling such tools. Our constructed agentic factor is the aggregate weekly log growth of this token consumption.

We define the agentic factor as the weekly log growth of aggregate agentic tokens.33 3 We define a week to be from Monday to Sunday. For each model response, OpenRouter records whether the model ends its turn by calling an external software tool. Tool calls allow models to request actions such as querying a database, running code, or reading or writing a file. We define *agentic tokens* as the tokens associated with responses that end in a tool call. The agentic factor has a weekly standard deviation of about 36 percent. Additionally, in order to measure broad AI token consumption as opposed to agentic AI-specific token consumption, we consider the AI factor of Borri et al. (2026), defined as the first principal component of standardized weekly log growth in total tokens, dollar expenditure, and the weekly average number of daily active users.

ultimate.title: The Cross-Section of Stock Returns and AI Exposure
ultimate.snippet:
The paper has four main parts. First, we build a high-frequency, time-varying AI factor from the full universe of OpenRouter AI token consumption data and decompose it into its important components: frontier closed-source versus open-weight models, core versus new users, seasoned versus casual users, long versus short prompts, prompt-content categories (e.g., programming, science, roleplay), and agentic versus ordinary requests. The AI factor and its different components show that the diffusion is uneven, token consumption is concentrated in programming, technology, and sciences, and the share of agentic tokens increased dramatically from negligible to more than half of total AI consumption.

Finally, we provide early evidence on the rise and market-implied effect of agentic AI consumption, defined as models executing multi-step workflows that plan, call external tools, take actions, and coordinate with other agents (see, e.g., Hassabis and Kavukcuoglu, 2024; Ng, 2024a; Ng, 2024b; Yang, Yonack, Zyskowski, Yarats, Ho and Ma, 2025). We measure this component in the OpenRouter data as requests in which the model invokes an external tool. We document the rise in the agentic token share from near zero in 2024 to roughly half of all tokens by the end of the sample, and the agentic dollar share rises more slowly as the realized price per agentic token falls. The granularity of the OpenRouter data allows us to track three salient token-level components of this activity: tool calls, the model’s internal reasoning tokens, and cache reads of recurring prompt prefixes. We show that tool-call and cache-read shares rise to roughly two-fifths to one-half of total token consumption, while reasoning tokens rise more slowly.
